'''''Saponaria officinalis''''' is a common [[perennial plant]] from the family [[Caryophyllaceae]]. This plant has many common names,<ref name=RHS>{{cite web |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1783 |title=Saponaria officinalis |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |website=Plant Selector |date=2002 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> including '''common soapwort''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 22 December 2017}}</ref> '''bouncing-bet''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''crow soap''',<ref name=RHS/> and '''soapweed'''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://science.halleyhosting.com/nature/gorge/5petal/pink/saponaria/officinalis.htm |title=The Pink Family in the Columbia River Gorge: Caryophyllaceae |first=Paul |last=Slichter}}</ref> There are about 20 species of [[soapwort]]s altogether.

The scientific name ''Saponaria'' is derived from the Latin {{wikt-lang|la|sapo}} (stem {{lang|la|sapon-}}) meaning "soap", which, like its common name, refers to its utility in [[Washing|cleaning]]. From this same Latin root is derived the name of the toxic substances [[saponin]]s found in many plants, including a specific saporin [[saponarin]] contained in the roots at levels up to 20 percent when the plant is flowering<ref>{{cite book |title=Farmakognosia |first1=Raimo |last1=Hiltunen |first2=Yvonne |last2=Holm |publisher=Helsinki University Press |language=Finnish}}</ref> (Indian soapnuts contain only 15 percent). The flowers colouring likely reflects the chemical environment of saponarin.<ref name="Takeda">Greenish blue flower colour of Strongylodon macrobotrys. Kosaku Takeda, Aki Fujii, Yohko Senda and Tsukasa Iwashina, Biochemical Systematics and Ecology, Volume 38, Issue 4, August 2010, Pages 630–633, {{doi|10.1016/j.bse.2010.07.014}}</ref> Saponins produce a lather when in contact with water. The epithet ''officinalis'' indicates its medicinal functions. It is a common host plant for some moth species, including the [[Hyles lineata|white-lined sphinx]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species/Hyles-lineata |title=White-lined Sphinx ''Hyles lineata'' (Fabricius, 1775) |website=Butterflies and Moths of North America |access-date=2017-11-14}}</ref>

''Saponaria officinalis''{{'}} native range extends throughout [[Europe]], and in [[Asia]] to western [[Siberia]]. It grows in cool places at low or moderate elevations under hedgerows and along the shoulders of roadways. It can be found as a horticultural escapee and noxious invasive in much of [[North America]].<ref>{{Minnesota Wildflowers|flower/bouncing-bet|Saponaria officinalis (Bouncing Bet) |access-date=2017-12-29}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Saponaria officinalis 018.jpg|thumb|left|Flowers, [[Sainte-Geneviève-de-Batiscan]], [[Quebec, Canada]]]]
The plant possesses leafy, unbranched [[Plant stem|stems]] (often tinged with red). It grows in patches, attaining a height of {{cvt|70|cm|in|0}}. The broad, [[lanceolate]], [[sessility (botany)|sessile]] [[leaf|leaves]] are opposite and between 4 and 12 cm long. Its sweetly scented [[flower]]s are [[radially symmetrical]] and pink, or sometimes white. Each of the five flat [[petal]]s have two small scales in the throat of the [[Corolla (flower)|corolla]]. They are about {{cvt|2.5|cm|in|frac=8}} wide. They are arranged in dense, terminal clusters on the main stem and its branches. The long tubular [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] has five pointed red teeth.

[[File:Saponaria officinalis Prague 2011 1.jpg|thumb|upright=1.36|A blooming clump at the [[Prague Botanical Garden]]]]
The individual flowers open in the evening, and stay open for about three days.<ref name=Wolff>{{cite journal|author1=Wolff, D. |author2=Witt, T. |author3=Jurgens, A. |author4=Gottsberger, G. |year=2006|title=Nectar dynamics and reproductive success in ''Saponaria officinalis'' (Caryophyllaceae) in southern Germany|journal=Flora. Morphologie, Geobotanik, Oekophysiologie|volume=201|issue=5|pages=353–364 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2005.07.010}}</ref> They produce a stronger scent at night and supplement nectar production during the night.<ref name=Wolff/> The flowers are protandrous: on the second night of blooming, the pollen is released, and the stigma develops to its final position by the third night.<ref name=Wolff/> Much of the seed production comes from self-pollination.<ref name=Wolff/> The flowers are visited by various insects including [[Noctuidae]], [[Sphingidae]], [[bumblebee]]s, and [[hoverfly|hoverflies]].<ref name=Wolff/>

In the [[Northern Hemisphere]] ''Saponaria officinalis'' blooms from May to September, and in the [[Southern Hemisphere]] October to March.

==External use==
As its common name implies, it can be used as a very gentle soap, usually in dilute solution. It has historically been used to clean delicate or unique [[textile]]s, especially [[woollen]] fabrics;<ref>[[Dioscorides]], ''The Herbal of Dioscorides the Greek'', Book 2:193, s.v. ''Strouthion''</ref> it has been hypothesized that the plant was used to treat the [[Shroud of Turin]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.shroud.com/pdfs/rogers.pdf | title = Shroud of Turin | access-date = 2012-06-03 }}</ref>

A lathery liquid that has the ability to dissolve fats or grease can be procured by boiling the leaves or roots in water.  Leaves are chopped, boiled, and strained; the liquid can then be used as soap.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mabey |first=Richard |title=Plants with a Purpose: A guide to the everyday use of wild plants |publisher=William Collins |date=1977}}</ref>

It has been widley used in Italy for skin conitions.<ref name="Chandra2021"/> In the Romanian village of [[Șieu-Odorhei]], natives call the plant {{lang|ro|săpunele}}. It is traditionally used by the villagers as a soap replacement for dry skin.{{citation needed|date=September 2020}}

==Internal use==
Saponins have long been known to cause throat irritation and have a bitter taste,<ref name="Oleszek2010">{{cite book|chapter= Saponin-Based Surfactants |last1=Oleszek|first1=W. |last2=Hamed, A|year=2010|pages=239-249|title=Surfactants from renewable resources|editor-first1=M. |editor-last1= Kjellin |editor-first2=I. |editor-last2=Johansson |isbn=978-0470760413}}</ref>{{rp|240}} and the maximum amount in food is regulated in many jurisdictions.<ref name="Oleszek2010"/>{{rp|242}} Some have medicinal uses and are well known plant toxins so an overdose could cause [[nausea]], [[diarrhea]], and [[vomiting]].<ref name="Oleszek2010"/>{{rp|243}}<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/all/saponaria-officinalis/ |title = Saponaria officinalis (Bouncing-bet, Soapwort) | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox}}</ref> Different types of saponins are synthesized by the species.<ref name="Chandra2021">{{cite journal|title=Phytochemistry and pharmacological activities of Saponaria officinalis L.: A review |last1=Chandra |first1=S. |last2=Rawat |first2=D.S. |last3=Bhatt |first3=A. |year=2021|journal=Notulae Scientia Biologicae |volume=13 |issue=1 |article-number=10809 |doi=10.15835/nsb13110809|doi-access=free }}</ref> The sapomin saponarin has low acute rat toxicity and no evidence of genotoxicity,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cho |first1=C.W. |last2=Song|first2=Y.R. |last3=Lim |first3=W.C. |last4=Hwang |first4=Y.H. |last5=Rhee |first5=Y.K. |last6=Choi |first6=J.W. |last7=Lee |first7=K.T. |last8=Hong |first8=H.D. |year=2020 |title=Acute oral toxicity and genotoxicity of polysaccharide fraction from young barley leaves (Hordeum vulgare L.) |journal=Foods |volume=9 |issue=6 |article-number=809 |doi=10.3390/foods9060809 |doi-access=free|pmc=7353472 }}</ref> so not all saponins are necessarily toxic when ingested.

Despite its toxic potential, ''Saponaria officinalis'' finds culinary use as an [[emulsifier]] in the commercial preparation of [[tahini]]<ref>{{cite book|first=Alice |last=Arndt |title=Seasoning Savvy: How to Cook With Herbs, Spices, and Other Flavorings |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WaPt5KSaVEIC&pg=PA215 |accessdate=3 June 2012 |date=10 August 1999 |publisher=Psychology Press |isbn=978-1-56022-031-2 |pages=215–}}</ref> and in brewing to create beer with a good [[beer head|head]]. In the Middle East, the root is often used as an additive in the process of making [[halva]]. The plant is used to stabilize the oils in the mixture and to create the distinctive texture of halva.

In traditional herbal medicine the roots of the species have been used as a diuretic. It was also used for coughs, bronchitis, stomach disorders,
bone deformations, rheumatism, pimples, skin diseases, bile disorders, liver problems and respiratory system diseases.<ref name="Chandra2021"/> 

Extracts from ''Saponaria officinalis'' have [[antioxidant]] properties and methanol extracts have [[antimicrobial]] actions against a wide range of bacteria including many human pathogens.<ref name="Chandra2021"/> A root extract is active against species of the pest plant mite ''[[Tetranychus urticae]]''.<ref name="Chandra2021"/> Ethanol extract inhibit the gastric enzyme [[hydrogen potassium ATPase]] that produces stomach acid.<ref>{{cite journal|title=In-Vitro Evaluation of Antiulcer Activity of Ethanol Extract of Saponaria Officinalis |last1=Sowmya |first1=M. |first2=S. |last2=Pavuluri|journal=Tropical Journal of Pharmaceutical and Life Sciences |volume=10 |issue= 5 |year=2023 |pages=12-17  |doi=10.61280/tjpls.v10i5.143|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Chemistry==
''Saponaria officinalis'' contains several saponins, which are [[ribosome-inactivating protein]]s. Amongst the saponins isolated with this property are isoform 6 of saponarin (SO6, saponin S6) from the seeds, and saporin-L1 (SAP) from the leaves.<ref name="Chandra2021"/> Saponariosides A,B, C, D, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, and M , vaccaroside D, dianchinenoside B, hydroxygypsogenic acid derivative compounds 1 and 2 and gypsogenic acid derivative compound 3 have been isolated from the whole plant or roots.<ref name="Chandra2021"/>
The many compounds responsible for the floral scent (predominantly [[methyl benzoate]]), and that compose essential oil extracts from the plant have also been characterised.<ref name="Chandra2021"/>

Saponin S6 is able to kill cancer cells via [[apoptosis]] and saporin SO1861 found in the plant increases the cytotoxicity of other compounds.<ref name="Chandra2021"/>
